urn with fire, and how at last one is lighted off to
bed with the jewels in the cup. Venus is not
visible when the comet is In sight. but sets early
In the evening, and Mars also sets too early to
be observed. Jupiter rises two hours before
midnight and glOws till morning. On the 18th

curry and Mars, with but half hours difference
between the points of nearest approach to the
planets With the telescope Neptune and


Uranus may be seen, but to the not too 1nuujsi-
tive person they are planets of no interest. The
great Kant once said that there were too things
that filled him with wonder and awe-the starry
heavens above him and the moral law within
him; but even people who feel no pressure of
the moral law within them must now be filled
with the awe and wonder Of the morning sky.

In terrible manner The round was finally

seventh and eighth rounds were knock downs

SAN Francisco, June 10. - The
pilot who took out the steamer Escam'
bia says that the water ballast tanks
had all been pumped ont to render the
ship lighter for carriage of cargo,
and that coal was stored on deck as
high as the bridge. While going down
the harbor the machinery was stopped
for few moments and the ship, falling
off into the trough of the sea, rolled the
scuppers under The pilot expressed
the opinion that she was unsafe, and
believes that the catastrophe might
have been expected in open water. The
disaster was seen from the signal station,
but it is impossible to say whether any
one was saved. The ships complement
consisted of about twenty-five men all
told. She was loaded by Dresback &
Co., and it is believed her cargo was
fully insured The Escambia was about
1000 tons, and came here from Hong
Kong, via Victoria, B. c., with Chinese
passengers.

The Democrats are everywhere having great
trouble with the temperance question. Here
tOfore they have been prOliting rather than
losing by i, for whenever the Temperance party
ran separate State ticket they worked in
directly but effectively in the interest or the
Democratic party The Democrats, while
not making open declaration of sympathy with
the liquor interests, were in close alliance
with them and were assured of all the votes
at their command. In this way they had the
aid of extreme temperance and antitemper-
ance people, while the Republicans, who were
the best friends the Temperance party ever
had. lost the votes of both. This situation
greatly delighted the Democrats, who looked
with much compacency upon the annual per
Torrance of the temperance people biting their
own noses oil.


This year, however, witnesses striking
change in the situation. The Temperance ana
Republican parties are working together Ill many
States, aud the Democrats find themselves III
a most perplcXing position. If they come out
openly i'll defence of the liquor sellers,
they invite overwhelming defeat, for in nearly
all the Western States the people are aroused
AS never before against free rum. If, on the
other hand, they assume a virtue, ana declare
in favor of temperance, they will ALLEVIATE the
liouor vote and cut themselves of from all
hope of victory. In States like Iowa it makes
little difference what position they take, for
they are certain of defeat anyway, but in Mainc
Ohio and Indiana the case is different If
they dodge the issue they are defeated and
if they take either side they are no better OIL
I'm Ohio they have lodged by meaningless
declaration against sumptuary laws. They
will face the question in Indiana tomorrow,
and will probably dodge again. There is ex-
cclent reason to believe that they will lose
both States by the naneuyre. In Maine they
are certain to be defeated anyway, and their
complete silence upon this absorbing question
will only magnify the disaster.


All this gives us great satisfaction. AT
last the Democracy is forced to the front in its
true character. 1t is aud always has been the
rum sellers party, and now that Justice has over
taken the rum-sellerS the party must share In
their punishment. There has not been bad cause
of any kind in this country since the party was
founded which it has not fostered in order to
gain its votes. Slavery, secession, reputation.
cheap money, Mormonism, Ku-KluXsm, free
rum-all have been nurSed and petted by the
Democracy sometimes openly sometimes
St cretly. One by one disaster has oyertaken
all, and whenever one goes down the glorious
old Democracy totters q little nearer to its
Grave.

THE CHINESE BILL PASSES THE SENATE.
fBY TELEGRAPH TO THE rRIBUsE.l


WASHINGTON. March 9.-The Chinese bill was
passed by the Senate to-day. The Ingalls, amend
ment reducing the time within which immigra-
tion shall be suspended, from twenty to ten
years, was rejected. Two amendments proposed by
Senator Farley. of California, prohibiting State
Courts from comforting citizenship upon Chinese
and decreeing that the prohibition Of immigration
should extend to skilled artisans as well as coolies
were adopted. Every effort to modify the bill in
accordance with the reasonable views of its Eastern
supporters rejected while the effort to make it
more severe than its original form was successful.


The Democrats voted in body. with the excep-
ton of Senator Brown, of Georgia, for the Farley
amendments and against the Ingalls, amendment.
The Republicans. with the exception of the
Pacific Coast Senators and Senator Cameron, of
Wisconsin, took tho opposite side The debate
throughout has been dignifed, and has shown upon
the part of Republican Senators creditable degree
of independence of thought and action. The con-
test was between sentiment upon the one side
that this country was rich enough and large enough
to furnish homes for all who might choose to come,
and upon the other that the Caucasian even in pow
erty demanded more for his labor than the mere
necessaries of life and refused to recognize as his
equal being who was content with bare existence


In return for his labor.


Two excellent speeches were made to-day, one by
Senator Hawley against the BILL and one by Senator
Jones, of Nevada, in its support A comparison of
the debate with that which took place when the
Fifteen Passenger bill, vetoed by President Hayes.
was under discussion, shows marked change in
the opinion of Senators, but the extreme views en-
tertaincd by Senator Farley, and embodied in his
amendments, would probably never have com.
manded the support of a majority of the Senate, had
not the Democrats surrendered their conviction to
the hope of political gain. The Republicans who
voted for the upon its final passage say that
these amendments were uncalled for, and were ir-
relevant to the subject matter of the bill

Col Robert G. Ingersoll delivered the follow
ing Grafton at the New York Academy of Music
Tuesday evening Decoration day. to an audi
ence of ten thousand people:


This day is sacred to our heroes dead Upon
their tOmbs we have lovingly laid the wealth of
spring. This is a day for memory and tears. A
mighty nation bends above it's honored graves
and pays to noble dust the tribute of it's love.
Gratitudeis the fairest flower that sheds its per
fume in the heart. To-day we tell the history of
our cOuntrys life; recount the lofty deeds Of
vanished years; the toll and suffering; the de-
feats and victories of heroic men-or men who
made our nation great and free. We see the
hrst ships whose prows were gilded by the
western sun. We feel the thrill of discovery
when the New World was found. We see the
oppressed, the serf, the peasant, and the slave
men whose flesh had known the chill of chains
the adventurous, the proud, the brave, sailing
an unknown sea, seeking homes in unknown
lands. We see the settlements, the little clear
ings, the block house and the fort. the rude and
lonely huts, brave men. true women, builders of
homes, fellers OffOrests founders of states Sep
arated from the Old World away from the
heartless distinctions Of caste, away from scep-
tiers and titles and crowns. they governed them
selves. They defended their homes, they earned
their bread. Each citizen had a voice, and the
little villages became almost republics Slowly
the savage was driven, foot by foot, back in the
dim forest. The days and nights were filled
with fear, and the slow years with massacre and
war, and the cabins earthen floors were wet
with blood of mothers and their babes But the
savages of the new world were kinder than the
kings and mobiles of the old; and so the human
tide kept coming, and the places of the dead
were filled. Amid common dangers and common
hopes the prejud ices and feuds of Europe faded
slowly from their hearts From every land. of
every speech, driven by want and lured BY hope.
eXileS and emigrants sought the mysterious
continent Of the west.


Year after year the coonists fought and toiled
and suffered and increased. They began to talk
about liberty-tO reason of the rights of man.
Ihey asked no help from distant kings. and they
began to doubt the use of paving tribute to the
useless, They lost respect for dukes and lords.
and held in high esteem all honest men, There
was the dawn OF a new day. They began to
dream of independence They found that they
could make ndeXecute the laws. They had tried
the experiment of self government They had
succeeded. The Old World wished to dominate
the New. In the care and keeping Of the colo
nists was the destiny of this cOntinent-of half
the world. On this day the story of the great
struggle between colOnists and kings should be
told. We should tell our children Of the con-
teSt-first for justice, then for freedom We
should tell them the history Of the Declaration
OF Independence, the chart and compass of all
human rlghts-"Ali men are equal and have the
right to life, to liberty" and joy. This declara-
ton uncrOwned kings and wrested from the
hands of titled tyranny the scepter of usurped
anil arbitrary power. 1t superseded royal grants
and repealed the cruel statutes of thousand
years. 1t gave the peasant a career 1t knight
ollfh
to fame and put the star of hope above the
cradle OF the poor mans babe. England was
then the mightiest of nations. mistress of every
sea. and yet our fathers. poor and few, defied
her power.


To-day we rememberthe defeats. the victories,
the disasters, the weary marches. the poverty,
the hunger, the sufferings, the agones. and
above all, the glOries Of the revolution We re-
member all-frOm Lexington to Valley Forge.
and from that midnight of despair to York
towns clOudiess day. We remember the SOL
diers and thinkers-the heroes of the sword and
pen. They had the brain and heart the wisdom
and the courage, to utter and defend these
words: Governments derive their just powers
| from the consent of the governed" In defense
OF this sublime and self-evident truth the war
was waged and won. To-day we remember all
the heroes. all the generous and chiyalric men
who came from other lands to make ours free.
VI the many thousands who shared the gloom
and glory OF the seven sacred years not one re-
MAINS The last has mingled with the earth.
and nearly all are sleeping now in unmarked
graves, and some beneath the leaning, crumbling
stones from which their names have been effaced
by Times irreverent and relentless hands
But the nation they founded remains The
United States. are still free and independent
The government derives it's just powers from
| the consent of the governed" and fifty million
OF free people remember with gratitude the
heroes of the revolution. Let us be truthful:
let US be kind. When peace came when the in
dependence of new nation was acknowledged.
| the great truth for which our fathers fought
was half denied, and the Constitution was incOn-
sistent with the Declaration. The war was
waged for liberty. and yet the victors forged
new letters for their fellOw-men. The chains
our fathers broke were put by them upon the
limbs OF others. FreedOm-fOr-all was the cloud
by day and the pillar of fire by night through
seven years Of want and war. In peace the
cloud was forgotten. and the pillar blazed I'M
seen. Let us be truthful; all of our fathers were
not true to themselves. In war they had been
generous, noble and self-sacrificing; with peace
great enough to appreciate the grandeur of the
principles for which they fought. They ceased
to regard the great truths as having universal
application. Liberty for ALL included only
themselves. They qualified the Declaration.
they interpolated the word ''white;" they oblit-
Grated the word ''all." Let us be kind. We
will remember the age in which they lived. We
will compare them with the citizens of other
nations.


They made merchandise of men. They legal
lied crime. They sOwed the seeds of war; but
they founded this nation.


Let us gratefully remember:
Let us gratefully forget


To-day we remember the heroes of the second
war with England, in which our fathers fought
for the freedom of the SEAS for the rights of the
American sailor We remember with pride the
splendid victories of Erie and Champlain. and
the wondn0us achievements upon the sea-
achievements that covered our navy with glory
that neither the victories nor defeats of the flu
ture can dim. We remember the heroic services
and sufferings of those who fought the merci-
less savage OF the frontier. We see the mid
night massacre and hear the war cries of the
allies Of England. We see the flames climb
round the happy homes, and in the charred and
blackened ruins we see the mutilated bodies OF
wives and children. Peace came at last, crowned
with the victory of New Orleans victory that
did redeem all sorrows" and all defeats. The
revolution gave our fathers a free land-the
war of 1912 a free sea. To-day we remember
the gallant men who bore our flag in triumph
from the Rio Grande to the heights of Chapul-
tepec.

rites over the remains of Ralph Waldo

formed and the body taken to the
Unitarian Church. Judge lockwood
delivered the address. Selections from

interesting address upon the life and
works of Emerson. A prayer and
benediction closed the exercises in the
church. The coffin was borne to the
cemetery where Rev. d. Haskins, Epis-

family, read the Episcopal burial service

A letter to the San Francisco Chron-
icle from Separ Station, gives a graphic
account of the slaughter of Loco's band
by the Mexicans who were under Gar
cia. 1t says: The Indians were pur-
sued by General Forsythe for thirty
miles across the Mexican border and
close to the Hannas river in Mexico,
where about 250 Mexican troops, be-
longing to General Terassas' command,
were concealed in small willow-fringed
creek, tributary of the Hannas river.
The Indians, unaware of the ambush
into which they were being driven, fell
into the trap. The Mexicans lay per-
fectly quiet until the Indians were
within hundred yards of them, and
then poured in sudden and murderous
fire. The destruction was almost COM
plete. Sixty warriors fell at the first
volley. The young and vigorous war
riors scattered and hunted cover. The
Mexican soldiers then charged upon the
old bucks, squaws and papooses, who
formed the center of the column. None
were spared. Squaws were bayoneted,
and the children and babes were taken
up by the heels and their brains dashed
out against the rocks. One old gray
headed Indian died game. He was con-
cealed in hole amongst the roots of
large willow, and succeeded in killing
eight of the Mexicans before they could
discover where the shots came from. He
was finally dragged out and completely
cut to pieces. counted seventy nine
dead squaws and papooses. Loco was
killed and Ju severely hurt.

palling storm disaster occurred Monday
night, near McAllister. AS the wires
are down for miles full details cannot
yet be learned. Reports of the extent
of the storm are conflicting, but the most
reliable is that eight persons were killed
outright and forty wounded. Many of
the latter will die. 1t is certain that
this number is no way exaggerated, and
the probability is that the fatalities and
casualties are much larger. The disas-
ter occurred at the coal mines, three
miles from McAllster Station, on the
Missouri, Kansas 4 Texas Railroad. The
storms came from the southwest and
southeast in triangular shape, and ap-
peared to meet and center near McAllis-
ter. A great deal of damage was done
near Paris. The buildings at the Nc
Allister mines were completely demol-
ished. Temporary buildings have been
arranged for the dead and wounded.
Physicians have gone up from here, and
all the aid possible will be sent forward.
The storm extended generally through
Texas, Arkansas and the Indian Terri
tory. Railroad travel is suspended in
nearly all directions by washouts. There
Was great hail-fall with the storm,
which extended as far north as Fort
Gibson.

Having for over fifteen years studied the
botany and carefully collected all the plants
of Dallas county, l can report pretty accu-
rately about its flora.


Omitting the inferior cryptogamous plants
such as moses, lichens, etc., and counting
only Homogeneous and vascular cryp-
togamous ferns), | have found lob
species distributed in lO2 orders and AGO
genera; seventy-one species have been in
troduced since the settlement of the coun-
try, and grow spontaneously now, and
probably few disappeared before
The ADVENT of civilization. We have
forty-four species of trees, more
or less large and about as many shrubs.
Among the more useful trees will men
ton the bois dare, (maclura aurantiaca)
the black walnut Guglans nigra) and the
red cedar ,1uniPerus yirglnlanusl; the
latter being the only representative OF the
order of conifera (pine, fir, etc. There are
eight species of oaks, four hickories. three
elms. Among the climbing shrubs the
more important. are several species and
varieties of grapes, from which tolerably
good wine is made-one, the winter grape
wits cordifolia) has been found perfectly
phylloxera proof and for that reason is in
great demand in Europe to be used as stock
to craft on the best varieties.


The character of our flora is western.
Few of the semi-tropical plants have
reached our region; such as the palmetto,
found in the eastern part of the country.
We have not SO good variety OF large
trees, such as those that make the bulk of
the forests in eastern Texas, nor have we
the numerous thorny shrubs and cacti that
characterize the region Of the southwest.


Our flora is very rich and offers good
many interesting species. A great variety
of beautiful flowers that have found their
way into the gardens of Europe are natives
of our soil; such are the Indian plume (gilia
geographically, the cardinal flower uobelia
the queen of the night (ment-
zelia ornata), the Eustylis purpurea, and
many others too numerous to mention.
Many native grasses and forage plants may
become the element of excellent artificial
pastures. Several fibre plants are also
found; among these is the flax, Of which !
found six species. No doubt good medici.
nal or otherwise useful plants can be found
when more properly observed.


JULIEN REvERCHoN,


Botanist.
ROSE COTTAGE, near Dallas, March 8, 1852.

toes have been used occasionally, partic-
ularly in the treatment of certain foot
troubles. Lately they have come into
more general use, and not little public
discussion has arisen over the fashiona-
BILE novelty. The London medical au-
thority Lancet is strongly inclined to
favor them as likely to conduce to COM
fort, and spare many persons who now
suffer from the development of soft corns
between the toes, serious trouble.
"They also would be more cleanly than
the stockings in common use, because
they would naturally absorb and re-
move the acrid moisture which accumu-
lates between the toes, and which is the
general cause of offensive odors from the
feet. They will, moreover, give the foot
better play, allowing its phalanges great
er freedom of action. And, lastly, a
we'll fitted digitated sock or stocking
will remove mass of material from the
toe of the boot, and, at the same time,
secure increased breadth and space for
expansion across the base of the toes.
The new stockings, supposing them to
be well cut and fitted, possess many
advantages"


Even if the toed stocking should have
no other effect than to expel the ugly
and unphysiological French toed" boot,
it would prove public benefit,

DIR. Holmes lately returned to Viz
ginia City from two weeks visit to
Coloma, California, his old-time mining
camp, and gave the Enterprise data for
the following: "Coloma is the spot
where gold was discovered in California,
but its glory as place of mining has long
since departed. 1t is now place of
orchards and vineyards. Although sur
rounded by'snowy mountains snow sell
dom falls in Coloma. There grow the
fig and the almond tree, and there flow
ers bloom every month in the year. The
people live in the vine embowered cot
tages, till their gardens, train their vines,
prune their trees and are happy, giving
no thought to underground wealth that
lies deeper than hill of potatoes. The
only miners now seen about Coloma are
Chinese Under the orchards and gar
dens is still a considerable amount of
ground that the pick has never disturbed.
The Chinese occasionally get upon leads
of gravel that run into these, and the
high prices they are willing to pay for a
small strip of garden or orchard shows
that they find the ground productive.
One man has, year after year, disposed
of slices of his orchard, and only the
other day sold for $500 the ground on
which stood four apple trees"
